These series are mostly familiar within SCD on a broad and overall level. They make up a lot of the commonly used reading/scaling material in SCD. The main reference pool is
Classroom of the elite, Tomodachi Game, Death Note (the big three ), Liar Game, Usogui, and Monster
Code Geass, The Mentalist, and Danganronpa
are used more occasionally or as supplementary references.
The reference pool and its series have characters across many different tiers and levels, making them useful for comparing and scaling characters against each other.
Familiarity here generally means broad knowledge of the series and its SCD-relevant material, rather than knowing every feat or interpretation in depth.
Reasons why I'm referring to TG, COTE, and DN  as the  big three are:
. COTE has digestible and diegetic hierarchy & dynamic of smart characters, TG has digestible and diegetic games & mind games, and DN has diegetic and digestible opposition and difficulty.

In other words, these series don't just have characters who are called smart. Their stories diegetically demonstrate and establish intelligence through games, conflicts, hierarchies, opposition, strategies, and interactions between characters.

This makes TG, COTE, and DN useful starting points for newer people to center themselves around when learning SCD. They provide recognizable examples of different types of intelligence and outsmarting while also giving people material that can be directly examined and scaled.
Plus, most people already have a general understanding of these series and characters, making it easier to learn by
— you don't necessarily need to read the entire series yourself to have a basic understanding of the characters, their feats, and their general scaling.

This doesn't mean these three series are inherently superior to everything else. They're being used primarily because of their popularity, familiarity, diegetic material, and usefulness as reference points.

Difficulties of an outcome are given estimations by the person scaling the characters in question.
- Implies the difficulty could be higher than what is estimated.
- Implies the difficulty could be lower than what is estimated.
Will take a standard character A vs B matchup for reference:

Almost nothing would be able to change the outcome of this match. Character A would have every winning condition and be significantly stronger than Character B in almost, if not, every aspect. Character A should still be able to guarantee victory even if they were to self-sabotage or to place themselves at a massive disadvantage.

This means that Character A’s victory would provide little challenge at all. Even their basic skill set would be enough to ensure victory. At this point, for example, even if Character A were to put himself at a massive disadvantage, that would do little to help Character B’s chances of winning given the massive overall difference in skill.

This means that Character A would not need to put forth their full effort to guarantee victory. This could also mean that Character A is superior to Character B is most or all facets of outsmarting. In that case Character A wouldn’t have a weakness that could even potentially allow Character B to win. Character A could ensure victory even from a disadvantageous position.

– This means that an average showing from Character A is enough to guarantee victory over Character B. They wouldn’t likely need to utilize their top end skills to ensure their win and Character B even with their best showing wouldn’t have a chance to win.
Character A would need to utilize their full potential, but doing so would guarantee their victory. Character A using their full skillset and effort will ensure they come out ahead.

Character A would need to use their full skillset and be fully prepared against an opponent who isn’t too far below them. However, as long as they don’t underestimate Character B, their full effort will be enough to ensure their win. It will take Character A’s best showing to ensure this. Despite this being close Character A’s efforts should manage to beat Character B.

This means that Character A’s victory would prove to be extremely difficult to guarantee, this represents the highest level of opponent they could beat more often than not. Situation variety and context are almost as relevant as they can ever be in determining the winner, as for example Character A may be superior to character B in some facets of outsmarting, but Character B might counter Character A very well. This could also be opposite where Character A counters well despite a slightly inferior skillset.

Represents a 50/50 matchup. In this case the matchup is too close to declare an overall winner. Neither character’s full effort would be enough to guarantee victory against the other without some kind of additional circumstances. One character ever so slightly underestimating the other for example may be the difference between victory and defeat.
